summary.text: The thermosphere is the layer of Earth's atmosphere above the mesosphere and below the exosphere, beginning about 80 km above sea level.
It absorbs highly energetic solar radiation, so its thin gas can reach 2,000 °C or more, yet an object there feels cold because the gas is too sparse to conduct heat.
Radiation electrically charges its particles, so most of the ionosphere lies here, and radio waves can be refracted and received beyond the horizon.

items.prompt: A thermometer hangs in the thermosphere, where the gas itself can reach 2,000 °C. What does it read at night?

options.label: Well below freezing
Close to 2,000 °C
About room temperature
Hot enough to melt it

items.explain: The gas is so thin that it barely passes heat to the thermometer, which loses more energy by radiation than it gains, so it reads far below 0 °C.

items.prompt: Thermosphere temperatures can change a great deal over time. What do they depend on most?

options.label: How much ozone lies below
Earth's distance from the Sun
How active the Sun is
The strength of ocean currents

items.explain: The layer is heated by highly energetic solar radiation, so its temperatures depend strongly on solar activity.

items.prompt: A loudspeaker is switched on at 200 km altitude. Why would nobody nearby hear it?

options.label: The cold freezes the speaker's parts
Molecules there collide too rarely to pass it on
Charged particles soak up the vibrations
Strong winds carry the noise away

items.explain: Above 160 km the gas is so thin that molecular interactions are too infrequent to transmit sound.

items.prompt: A ham radio operator chats with someone far beyond the horizon. What in the thermosphere makes this possible?

options.label: Ozone that reflects light back down
Cold air that carries signals farther
Satellites relaying every amateur call
Charged particles that bend the signal

items.explain: Radiation makes the particles in this layer electrically charged, which lets radio waves be refracted and received beyond the horizon.

items.prompt: Low down, nitrogen and oxygen stay evenly mixed. High in the thermosphere, how do the gases arrange themselves instead?

options.label: They form a single uniform blend
Heavier gases float to the top
They sort by weight, lighter ones higher
They all turn into charged ions

items.explain: Above the turbopause, gases separate by molecular mass, and lighter ones such as atomic oxygen, helium and hydrogen dominate higher up.

items.prompt: The thermosphere is extremely hot. Why does it have almost no effect on the energy of the air below it?

options.label: The ozone layer reflects its heat away
It holds only a tiny fraction of the air's mass
Its heat only reaches it at night
The mesosphere absorbs all its warmth

items.explain: The thermosphere holds only 0.002% of the atmosphere's mass, so no significant energetic feedback to the lower regions is expected.

paragraphs.heading: Above the mesosphere
paragraphs.text: The thermosphere is the layer of Earth's atmosphere just above the mesosphere and below the exosphere. Its name comes from the Greek word for heat, and it begins about 80 km above sea level. Its upper border, the thermopause, separates it from the exosphere, which begins about 600 km up and is where the atmosphere turns into outer space. By the definition of the Kármán line, set at 100 km, most of the thermosphere already counts as space.

paragraphs.heading: Hot gas that feels cold
paragraphs.text: Temperatures here rise with height, because the gas absorbs highly energetic radiation from the Sun. They depend strongly on solar activity and can climb to 2,000 °C or more, and the very thin gas can reach 2,500 °C. Yet an object in the thermosphere would feel cold. The gas is so sparse, practically a hard vacuum, that its molecules cannot conduct heat to it. At night a normal thermometer would read well below 0 °C, since it would lose more energy by radiating than it picks up by touching the gas.

paragraphs.heading: Charged air and radio
paragraphs.text: Ultraviolet light breaks molecules apart and ionizes them, creating ions, so the bulk of the ionosphere lies inside the thermosphere. Because radiation leaves the particles here electrically charged, radio waves can be refracted by them and picked up beyond the horizon. The Sun's X-rays and extreme ultraviolet light, at wavelengths below 170 nm, are almost entirely absorbed in this layer.

paragraphs.heading: Gases sorted by weight
paragraphs.text: Below the turbopause, at about 90 km, turbulence keeps the air a well-mixed blend whose composition does not change, dominated by nitrogen (N₂) and oxygen (O₂). Above it, the gases separate according to their molecular mass, each thinning with height at its own rate. Above about 200 km, lighter gases take over one after another: atomic oxygen (O), then helium (He), then hydrogen (H). Their balance shifts with location, time and solar activity.

paragraphs.heading: Very little mass
paragraphs.text: The density of the atmosphere falls off almost exponentially as you go up. About 80 percent of the atmosphere's mass sits in the troposphere, while everything above about 85 km holds only 0.002 percent of it. With so little mass, the thermosphere cannot be expected to send any significant energy back down to the layers below.

paragraphs.heading: Silence and space stations
paragraphs.text: Above 160 km, in what is called the anacoustic zone, molecules meet so rarely that sound cannot travel. The way this layer moves is dominated by atmospheric tides, driven mainly by daily heating. The thermosphere has no inhabitants except two space stations. The International Space Station orbits in the middle of it, 408 to 410 km up, and the Tiangong station orbits between 340 and 450 km.
